title: Inverse Functions
summary: An inverse function undoes another: if $f$ sends $a$ to $b$, then $f^{-1}$ sends $b$ back to $a$. A function has an inverse only if it's one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test); their graphs mirror across $y=x$.

one-to-one.plain: Each output comes from a single input.

horizontal line test.plain: No horizontal line hits the graph twice.

swap x and y.plain: The algebra for finding an inverse.

reflection over y=x.plain: Inverse graphs mirror across this line.

domain/range swap.plain: Inverse's domain is the original's range.

restricting the domain.plain: Limiting inputs to make a function invertible.

concept_sections.heading: What an inverse does
concept_sections.explanation: The inverse reverses the mapping: $f^{-1}$ takes outputs back to inputs, so $f^{-1}(f(x))=x$ and $f(f^{-1}(x))=x$.

concept_sections.heading: One-to-one functions
concept_sections.explanation: Only one-to-one functions (each output from a unique input) have inverses. The horizontal line test checks this on a graph.
math_steps: Check each output has one input.

concept_sections.heading: Finding an inverse algebraically
concept_sections.explanation: Write $y=f(x)$, swap $x$ and $y$, then solve for $y$: that's $f^{-1}(x)$.

concept_sections.heading: Graphs and domains
concept_sections.explanation: Inverse graphs are reflections across $y=x$; the inverse's domain and range are the original's range and domain, swapped.

concept_sections.heading: Restricting the domain
concept_sections.explanation: Functions that aren't one-to-one (like $x^2$) become invertible on a restricted domain (like $x\ge0$), giving a valid inverse there.
